title: Family arti

segments.voice: Yesterday, taking the light: hands over the flame, then to the eyes. Your line was take it. Did you let someone's kindness land, without waving it away? Day one hundred and twenty-two.

Ask people who grew up with evening arti what they remember, and it's rarely the words. It's who was there. Dad holding the plate a little too high. A little sister fighting to ring the bell, and ringing it the entire time. An aunt singing half a beat ahead of everyone. The smell of camphor, and dinner waiting in the next room. For ten minutes, the whole house was facing the same way. This week you've learned the hour, the flame, the song and the light. All of it works alone. But arti was built for more than one. Today: family arti.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE REMEMBER: WHO WAS THERE.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE FACING ONE WAY.` → `TODAY: FAMILY ARTI.`

segments.voice: Look at how arti is put together and you'll see it almost asks for company. It has jobs. Someone holds the lamp. Someone rings the bell, often the youngest, because it's the best job. Everyone sings. Then the plate goes around, and each person takes the light. Even the smallest child has something to do. That's by design. Hindu tradition names four stages of life, and the second, the householder, grihastha, is the one lived in a home full of people. Many teachers have praised it as the stage that holds up the others, because the household is where the feeding, the raising, the caring for elders all happen. And the home shrine sits right in the middle of it. Worship isn't something you leave the house to do; the house is where it's done. So evening arti becomes a kind of daily meeting. The day's arguments get paused. The phones go down, or at least face down. For ten minutes, whoever is under that roof stands together in front of one flame. Now, real families are complicated. Some people live alone. Some live with a partner from another faith, or with none. Nobody here is saying anyone has to join. A guest can simply stand in the room, listen and watch. But the invitation matters. People say you can pray alone anywhere. Arti, done together, adds something else. It's one of the ways a house becomes a home.
screen: `ARTI HAS JOBS: LAMP, BELL, SONG.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER: GRIHASTHA.` · `THE HOUSE IS WHERE IT'S DONE.` · `NO ONE HAS TO. EVERYONE IS ASKED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one person you could invite to do this with you, even once. A roommate, a parent on a video call, a partner, a child, a friend. Picture them in the room with you: one of you holds the flame, one rings the bell. Notice how it feels to not be the only one facing the light. Then think of how you might ask them, simply, with no pressure at all. If they say no, that's fine too. The bell holds the time.
Family arti. Arti done together: one lamp, one bell, one song, and a job for everyone in the house. Today's word.
Your line: one more. Today, ask one more person to join something you usually do alone: a walk, a meal, a minute of quiet, the flame. Day one hundred and twenty-two.

howItsDone: In many Hindu homes, evening arti is a family gathering: one person circles the lamp, a child often rings the bell, everyone sings, and the lamp is passed around so each person can take the light.

original.note: Sanskrit gṛhastha: the householder, the second of the four stages of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: one person's private ritual.
what it means: a ritual with jobs for everyone, a daily meeting where the whole house faces the same way.

what a scholar hears: the ashrama system names four life stages, and texts such as the Manusmriti praise the householder as the support of the others; home worship keeps the grihastha's house as a center of religious life.

sources.ref: The four ashramas; the householder as the support of the other stages (e.g., Manusmriti 3.77–78)
